patient.name: Kenneth Okafor
patient.setting: Orthopaedic ward, day 5 after hip surgery
patient.complaint: New fever, cough and breathlessness five days after a hip hemiarthroplasty
background: Fractured neck of femur after a fall at home in Catford
Urinary catheter and peripheral cannula since admission

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely causative organism?' in an inpatient: the timing (48 hours or more after admission), the device and recent antibiotics point to the type and the bug.

points: Kenneth, 76, had a hip hemiarthroplasty **5 days ago**.
Today: fever, productive cough and new breathlessness.
Catheter still in; wound looks clean and dry.

steps.lead: Kenneth's fever started **5 days after admission**, well past 48 hours, with no community source: this is hospital-acquired.

visual.title: Hours after admission when symptoms began
visual.label: Kenneth 120 h
visual.caption: The 48-hour line decides CAP vs HAP, and so the antibiotic.

steps.lead: Kenneth's biggest risk is **being in hospital**, plus surgery, a catheter, a cannula and diabetes.
New fever and cough on the ward: hospital organisms are more **resistant**, such as MRSA and Gram-negatives.

steps.q: Kenneth's cough and fever began on day 5. Which diagnosis fits best?
steps.r: Fever, productive cough and crackles **48 hours or more** after admission is **HAP**. Atelectasis gives low-grade fever in the first day or two.

visual.title: Portable chest X-ray, day 5
visual.caption: New right lower zone consolidation: hospital-acquired pneumonia.

steps.lead: Kenneth's RR 22 and SpO2 94% make this **non-severe HAP**. His catheter, wound and future line are other HAI sources to check.

steps.title: Spot the hospital infection
head: Type
Clue in the stem
Usual organism
rows: Cough, fever, new CXR shadow ≥48 h
Central line, rigors, red exit site

steps.text: Fever on **day 1** of an admission is community-acquired, even on a ward. Use the **48-hour** rule, not where the patient is now.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' with the answer usually blood cultures (and the relevant sample) before antibiotics; the gold standard is a positive culture with the clinical picture.

steps.q: Which must be done before Kenneth's first antibiotic dose?
steps.r: **Blood cultures** (and sputum) go before antibiotics in suspected hospital-acquired infection, so the culture is not sterilised.

steps.lead: Kenneth gets blood cultures, a **sputum sample**, a catheter urine sample, FBC, CRP and a CXR before antibiotics start.

steps.title: Bloods, day 5
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers; normal lactate, so no septic shock.

steps.title: Sample before you treat
nodes: Site sample: sputum, catheter urine, wound swab
Imaging: CXR, or USS/CT for abscess
steps.caption: Do not delay antibiotics in sepsis, but take cultures first where possible.

steps.lead: Kenneth's diagnosis is confirmed when a **positive culture** matches the clinical picture.

steps.title: Microbiology, day 7
steps.text: The culture fits the pneumonia, so treatment continues unchanged.
In a catheterised patient a **urine dipstick is unreliable**: send a catheter urine sample for culture instead.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' testing the drug: non-severe HAP = co-amoxiclav, severe HAP = piperacillin-tazobactam, first C. difficile = oral vancomycin, recurrence within 12 weeks = fidaxomicin; plus source control.

steps.q: Kenneth has non-severe HAP. Which antibiotic fits these notes?
steps.r: Non-severe HAP: **co-amoxiclav**. Piperacillin-tazobactam is kept for severe HAP (tachypnoea, hypoxia, sepsis).

steps.lead: Kenneth starts **co-amoxiclav** after cultures. Had he been hypoxic at 91% with RR 26, it would be **piperacillin-tazobactam**.

visual.title: Response to co-amoxiclav
visual.caption: Pneumonia settling by day 8. Then on day 9 the diarrhoea starts.

points: Day 9: Kenneth has **seven watery stools** in 24 hours.
He has been on co-amoxiclav for 4 days.
Stool sample sent; moved to a **side room**.

steps.title: Stool and bloods, day 9
steps.text: Toxin-positive C. difficile infection after antibiotics.

steps.q: This is Kenneth's first episode. Which treatment?
steps.r: First episode: **oral vancomycin**. Fidaxomicin is for recurrence within 12 weeks; loperamide is avoided.

steps.lead: If Kenneth's diarrhoea comes back **within 12 weeks**, he gets **oral fidaxomicin**, which reduces further recurrence better than vancomycin.
Kenneth is **isolated** in a side room; his catheter is removed as soon as he no longer needs it, and staff wash hands each contact.

steps.text: Alcohol gel does **not** kill C. difficile spores. Use **soap and water** and gloves and apron for C. difficile patients.

steps.lead: If Kenneth became febrile and hypotensive, that is **hospital-acquired sepsis**: Sepsis Six within the hour.
Kenneth's care follows **NICE NG139** for preventing healthcare-associated infection and NICE guidance on C. difficile.

science.exam: Expect applied science: why devices cause infection (biofilm), why antibiotics cause C. difficile, how MRSA resists beta-lactams (mecA, PBP2a) and why ventilation leads to Pseudomonas pneumonia.

points: Kenneth's daughter asks why he caught two infections in hospital.
You explain host, organism and device.

steps.lead: Kenneth is a **vulnerable host** (age, surgery, diabetes) exposed to **hospital-adapted**, more resistant flora.
His **urinary catheter** breaches a barrier and grows a **biofilm**, which shields bacteria from immunity and antibiotics.
Kenneth's co-amoxiclav wiped out normal gut flora, letting **C. difficile** spores germinate and release **toxins A and B**.

steps.title: How antibiotics lead to C. difficile

steps.q: A wound swab from the next bay grows MRSA. Why does it resist flucloxacillin?
steps.r: **mecA** encodes **PBP2a**, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams, so cell-wall synthesis continues.

steps.lead: Any S. aureus in Kenneth's wound would need a different drug if it carried **mecA**; flucloxacillin would fail.
Kenneth is not ventilated, but in ICU **micro-aspiration** around the tube cuff seeds the lungs with **Pseudomonas**.

steps.text: Ventilator-associated pneumonia's classic organism is **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**, a Gram-negative rod; CAUTI's is **E. coli**.

mcq.q: After how long in hospital is an infection classed as hospital-acquired?
mcq.r: Infection starting 48 hours or more after admission.

mcq.q: What is the most important risk factor for hospital-acquired infection?
mcq.r: Being in hospital is the biggest single risk, then devices and surgery.

mcq.q: Which organism most commonly causes catheter-associated UTI?
mcq.r: E. coli is the commonest CAUTI organism.

mcq.q: Which organism is the leading cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia?
What must be sent before starting antibiotics for suspected HAP?
o: Blood cultures and lower respiratory samples
mcq.r: Peripheral blood cultures and respiratory samples first.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard for confirming a hospital-acquired infection?
o: Positive culture with the clinical picture
mcq.r: A positive culture combined with the clinical picture.

mcq.q: Which antibiotic is used for severe HAP?
mcq.r: Severe HAP: IV piperacillin-tazobactam; non-severe: co-amoxiclav.

mcq.q: What is the first-line treatment for a first episode of C. difficile?
mcq.r: Oral vancomycin for the initial episode.

mcq.q: Which drug treats C. difficile recurrence within 12 weeks?
mcq.r: Fidaxomicin reduces further recurrence better than vancomycin.
mecA encodes PBP2a, which has low affinity for beta-lactams.

prompts.q: What defines a hospital-acquired infection and who is at risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check the day of admission in the stem before naming the infection.

points.p: Infection starting 48 hours or more after admission
points.why: Under 48 hours is community-acquired, even on a ward.

points.p: No evidence of a community source
points.why: It was not incubating on arrival.

points.p: Biggest risk factor: hospitalisation itself
Devices, surgery and immunosuppression

prompts.q: List the main types of hospital-acquired infection and the clue for each.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the device or drug in the stem names the infection.

points.p: HAP and VAP: cough, fever, breathlessness 48 hours or more after admission
points.why: VAP happens in ventilated ICU patients.

points.p: CAUTI: dysuria and fever with an indwelling urinary catheter
points.why: The catheter is the key risk factor.

points.p: Surgical site infection: red, painful, discharging wound after surgery
C. difficile: diarrhoea after antibiotics
Line sepsis: fever and sepsis from a central venous catheter
points.why: Look for redness or pus at the exit site.

prompts.q: How do you tell severe from non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: severity decides the antibiotic.

points.p: Severe: tachypnoea, e.g. RR 26
points.why: Raised RR is an early warning sign.

points.p: Severe: hypoxia, e.g. SpO2 91% on air
Severe: fever and signs of sepsis
Non-severe: normal saturations and RR, no sepsis

prompts.q: Name the classic organisms of hospital-acquired infection.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'most likely causative organism' is a favourite lead-in.

points.p: Overall: Staphylococcus aureus, especially MRSA
VAP/HAP: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
CAUTI: E. coli
Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea: Clostridioides difficile

prompts.q: What investigations do you send for a suspected hospital-acquired infection?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cultures before antibiotics where possible.

points.p: Blood cultures in any suspected hospital-acquired sepsis
Urine and sputum culture from the likely source
Imaging: CXR for pneumonia, USS or CT for abscess
FBC and CRP
Gold standard: positive culture with the clinical picture
points.why: A positive culture alone may be a contaminant.

prompts.q: Which empirical antibiotics are used for HAP?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: read the observations to grade severity, then pick the drug.

points.p: Non-severe HAP: co-amoxiclav
Severe HAP: IV piperacillin-tazobactam
Cultures before antibiotics, then adjust to results

prompts.q: How is C. difficile infection treated, first episode and recurrence?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 12-week window decides vancomycin vs fidaxomicin.

points.p: First episode: oral vancomycin
points.why: Oral, because it acts in the gut lumen.

points.p: Recurrence within 12 weeks: oral fidaxomicin
Isolate the patient
points.why: Spores spread on hands and surfaces.

points.p: Stop or review the causative antibiotic

prompts.q: How are hospital-acquired infections controlled and prevented, and what is the emergency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: source control is the answer when antibiotics alone fail.

points.p: Source control: remove or replace infected catheter or line, drain abscess
points.why: Biofilm makes devices hard to sterilise.

points.p: Hand hygiene and aseptic technique for devices
Fever with hypotension = hospital-acquired sepsis: Sepsis Six

prompts.q: Why do indwelling devices and antibiotics predispose to infection?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the mechanism, biofilm or flora disruption.

points.p: Devices breach anatomical barriers
points.why: Skin or urethral defences are bypassed.

points.p: Devices provide a surface for biofilm
points.why: Biofilm protects bacteria from immunity and antibiotics.

points.p: Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt gut flora so C. difficile spores germinate
points.why: Clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, quinolones are high risk.

points.p: C. difficile toxins A and B cause colitis

prompts.q: How does MRSA resist beta-lactams, and why does ventilation cause pneumonia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mecA and micro-aspiration are the key phrases.

points.p: mecA gene encodes PBP2a with low affinity for beta-lactams
points.why: So flucloxacillin cannot bind and cell-wall synthesis continues.

points.p: Micro-aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions around the endotracheal tube cuff
points.why: The cuff does not seal perfectly.

points.p: Seeds the lungs with hospital flora such as Pseudomonas

glossary.HAP: Hospital-acquired pneumonia: pneumonia starting 48 hours or more after admission.
glossary.Hospital-acquired pneumonia: Pneumonia starting 48 hours or more after hospital admission.
glossary.VAP: Ventilator-associated pneumonia: pneumonia arising 48 hours or more after intubation.
glossary.Ventilator-associated pneumonia: Pneumonia arising in a patient on a ventilator, often from Pseudomonas.
glossary.CAUTI: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection, usually E. coli.
glossary.CAP: Community-acquired pneumonia: starts outside hospital or within 48 hours of admission.
glossary.Surgical site infection: Infection of an operation wound causing redness, pain and discharge.
glossary.Line sepsis: Bloodstream infection arising from a central venous catheter.
glossary.Central venous catheter: A line placed in a large central vein for drugs, nutrition or monitoring.
glossary.MRSA: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: resistant to beta-lactams such as flucloxacillin.
glossary.mecA: Gene that gives MRSA its resistance by encoding PBP2a.
glossary.PBP2a: Altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams, so the cell wall keeps being built.
glossary.Penicillin-binding protein: Bacterial enzyme that builds the cell wall; the target of beta-lactam antibiotics.
glossary.Beta-lactam: Antibiotic class including penicillins and cephalosporins that blocks cell-wall synthesis.
glossary.Biofilm: A slime layer of bacteria on a device surface that shields them from immunity and antibiotics.
glossary.C. difficile: Clostridioides difficile: spore-forming Gram-positive anaerobe causing antibiotic-associated colitis.
glossary.Clostridioides difficile: Spore-forming anaerobe that causes diarrhoea and colitis after antibiotics.
glossary.Toxins A and B: C. difficile toxins that damage the colon lining and cause colitis.
glossary.Pseudomembranous colitis: Severe C. difficile colitis with yellow plaques on the colon lining.
glossary.GDH: Glutamate dehydrogenase: a screening stool test for C. difficile, confirmed with a toxin test.
glossary.Fidaxomicin: Oral macrocyclic antibiotic for recurrent C. difficile; lower recurrence than vancomycin.
glossary.Vancomycin: Glycopeptide antibiotic; given orally for C. difficile because it stays in the gut.
glossary.Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; used for non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia.
glossary.Piperacillin-tazobactam: Broad-spectrum anti-Pseudomonal penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, for severe HAP.
glossary.Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Gram-negative rod; classic cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia.
glossary.Empirical antibiotics: Antibiotics started before culture results, based on the likely organism.
glossary.Source control: Removing the source of infection, such as an infected line, or draining an abscess.
glossary.Sepsis Six: Oxygen, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate and urine output within one hour.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.Micro-aspiration: Small-volume inhalation of secretions, e.g. leaking past an endotracheal tube cuff.
glossary.Endotracheal tube: A breathing tube passed into the trachea for mechanical ventilation.
glossary.Aseptic technique: Methods that prevent contamination when inserting or handling devices.
glossary.Isolation: Nursing an infectious patient in a side room to stop spread.
glossary.Coagulase-negative staphylococci: Skin staphylococci such as S. epidermidis that colonise lines and form biofilms.
glossary.Atelectasis: Collapse of small airways, common after surgery, causing low-grade fever in the first 48 hours.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: a blood marker of inflammation.
glossary.NICE NG139: NICE guideline on preventing healthcare-associated infections.

technique.stem: A 71 year old woman is on day 4 of an admission for a stroke. She develops a fever and a cough productive of green sputum. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There are coarse crackles at the left base.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: and the timing is in the first line.

clues: fever and a cough productive of green sputum
coarse crackles at the left base
steps.x: Day 4 is past 48 hours; infective respiratory picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pneumonia starting 48 hours or more after admission = **hospital-acquired pneumonia**.

elim: Atelectasis is early, low-grade and without purulent sputum.
CAP must start before or within 48 hours of admission.
PE gives pleuritic pain and hypoxia, not purulent sputum and crackles.
She has had no operation.

steps.x: **C. Hospital-acquired pneumonia.** Rule: ≥48 h after admission = HAP.

technique.stem: An 83 year old man has had a long-term urinary catheter for 2 months. He is admitted with new confusion, fever and suprapubic tenderness. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 126/72 mmHg. A dipstick of urine from the catheter bag shows leucocytes and nitrites.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: Confirming the diagnosis means culture from the source.

clues: dipstick of urine from the catheter bag
steps.x: CAUTI suspected; dipstick unreliable with a catheter.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gold standard is a **positive culture**: send a catheter urine specimen (ideally after changing the catheter).

elim: Blood cultures help if septic but do not confirm the urinary source alone.
CT KUB is for stones or obstruction.
Ultrasound looks for obstruction, not infection.
Dipsticks are unreliable in catheterised patients.

steps.x: **B. Catheter urine culture.** Rule: catheter + fever → culture, not dipstick.

technique.stem: A 79 year old woman had C. difficile infection 6 weeks ago, treated with oral vancomycin with full recovery. She now has eight watery stools a day and lower abdominal cramps. Stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Treatment of a repeat episode: note the timing.
Recurrence within 12 weeks of a first episode.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Recurrence within 12 weeks = **oral fidaxomicin**.

elim: Faecal transplant is for multiple recurrences.
IV metronidazole alone is not first choice.
Antimotility drugs are avoided in C. difficile.
Vancomycin is for the first episode; fidaxomicin reduces recurrence.

steps.x: **C. Oral fidaxomicin.** Rule: first = vancomycin; recurrence within 12 weeks = fidaxomicin.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has been intubated and ventilated on ICU for 6 days after a road traffic collision. He develops fever, purulent tracheal secretions and a new infiltrate on chest X-ray. Tracheal aspirate grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which this infection developed?
o: Haematogenous spread from a central line
Micro-aspiration of secretions around the tube cuff

steps.x: Mechanism of ventilator-associated pneumonia.
VAP, 48 hours or more after intubation, with hospital flora.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Secretions leak past the **endotracheal tube cuff** and seed the lungs.

elim: Line spread gives bacteraemia, not primary VAP.
He has been in ICU for 6 days; this is hospital flora.
Pseudomonas is not a latent infection.
Gut translocation causes bacteraemia, not this pneumonia.

steps.x: **C. Micro-aspiration around the cuff.** Rule: VAP = micro-aspiration of hospital flora, classically Pseudomonas.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman is on day 8 of an admission for cellulitis treated with clindamycin. She develops six episodes of watery diarrhoea a day with lower abdominal cramps. She has not vomited. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: diarrhoea in an inpatient.
Hospital onset, high-risk antibiotic, watery diarrhoea, raised WCC.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in hospital = **C. difficile infection**.

elim: Diverticulitis gives left iliac fossa pain, not watery diarrhoea after antibiotics.
Ischaemic colitis gives bloody diarrhoea in vascular patients.
Norovirus causes prominent vomiting in ward outbreaks.
UC is chronic bloody diarrhoea, not new after clindamycin.

steps.x: **A. C. difficile infection.** Rule: antibiotics + hospital + diarrhoea = C. difficile.

practice.e: Watery diarrhoea starting in hospital after clindamycin, with a raised WCC, is C. difficile infection. Norovirus would bring vomiting and affect others on the ward.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has had a urethral catheter since a prostatectomy 10 days ago. He develops fever, rigors and suprapubic pain. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. A catheter urine sample is sent for culture.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: Organism question: name the infection first.
Catheter in place for days, now urinary sepsis: CAUTI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Commonest CAUTI organism: **Escherichia coli**.

elim: Candida is seen with long-term antibiotics or immunosuppression, not first choice.
Enterococcus occurs in CAUTI but less often than E. coli.
Proteus is linked to stones and long-term catheters, less common.
S. epidermidis is a line and prosthesis organism.

steps.x: **C. Escherichia coli.** Rule: CAUTI = E. coli.

practice.e: Catheter-associated UTI is most often caused by E. coli. Proteus and Enterococcus occur but are less common; S. epidermidis is a line organism.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman receiving parenteral nutrition through a tunnelled central venous catheter for 3 weeks develops rigors when the line is flushed. The skin around the exit site is red and tender with a small amount of pus. Her chest is clear, the urine dipstick is negative and she has no wound.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: which hospital-acquired infection?

clues: rigors when the line is flushed
red and tender with a small amount of pus
steps.x: Central line, rigors on flushing, exit-site infection; other sources excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Line-related sepsis = **central line-associated bloodstream infection**.

elim: Urine dipstick negative and no urinary catheter.
Chest is clear.
Thrombophlebitis is a peripheral cannula vein problem without rigors on flushing.
She has no surgical wound.

steps.x: **B. Central line-associated bloodstream infection.** Rule: rigors on flushing a line = line sepsis.

practice.e: Rigors on flushing and pus at the exit site of a central venous catheter is a line-associated bloodstream infection. Other sources have been excluded.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has been ventilated on ICU for 5 days after a cardiac arrest. He develops a fever, rising oxygen requirements and green tracheal secretions. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. Tracheal aspirate shows Gram-negative rods.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: Organism question in a ventilated patient.
VAP with a Gram-negative rod.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: VAP's leading organism: **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**.

elim: H. influenzae is a COPD and community organism.
Legionella is community, linked to water systems and travel.
Mycoplasma is atypical community pneumonia in the young.
Strep. pneumoniae is the CAP organism and Gram-positive.

steps.x: **D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa.** Rule: VAP + Gram-negative rods = Pseudomonas.

practice.e: Ventilator-associated pneumonia with Gram-negative rods is most likely Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Strep. pneumoniae is a Gram-positive CAP organism.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man is 6 days after an open inguinal hernia repair. The wound is red, hot and painful with purulent discharge. A wound swab shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters resistant to flucloxacillin.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: Organism in a surgical site infection.

clues: 6 days after an open inguinal hernia repair
steps.x: Post-op wound infection; staphylococci; beta-lactam resistant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Staph resistant to flucloxacillin = **MRSA**.

elim: Streptococci form chains, not clusters.
MSSA would be flucloxacillin-sensitive.
Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative rod.
S. epidermidis rarely causes purulent wound infection; it colonises lines.

steps.x: **B. MRSA.** Rule: clusters + flucloxacillin resistance = MRSA.

practice.e: Gram-positive cocci in clusters resistant to flucloxacillin in a surgical wound is MRSA. MSSA is flucloxacillin-sensitive and streptococci grow in chains.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman develops a cough and fever on day 6 after a laparotomy. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. There is bronchial breathing at the right base. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis includes a severity: read the observations.

clues: bronchial breathing at the right base
steps.x: Day 6 = hospital-acquired; RR 26 and SpO2 91% = severe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tachypnoea and hypoxia make this **severe hospital-acquired pneumonia**.

elim: Pulmonary oedema is bilateral with no fever.
Day 6 is beyond 48 hours.
RR 26 and SpO2 91% are severe features.
PE gives a clear chest, not focal bronchial breathing and consolidation.

steps.x: **E. Severe HAP.** Rule: ≥48 h + tachypnoea and hypoxia = severe HAP.

practice.e: Pneumonia on day 6 is hospital-acquired, and RR 26 with SpO2 91% makes it severe. CAP would start before 48 hours.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man on day 5 of an admission for a hip fracture develops fever and productive cough. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. The team plans to start empirical antibiotics.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting antibiotics?

steps.x: Investigation before treatment.
Suspected HAP; antibiotics about to start.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Send **blood cultures** (plus sputum) before antibiotics.

elim: CTPA is for suspected PE.
D-dimer is for PE and non-specific after surgery.
Procalcitonin does not identify the organism.
Legionella antigen is a community test in severe CAP.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Rule: cultures before antibiotics in hospital-acquired infection.

practice.e: Peripheral blood cultures and respiratory samples should be sent before antibiotics for HAP so the organism can be identified and treatment narrowed.

practice.stem: A 77 year old woman on day 7 of treatment with co-amoxiclav for a hospital-acquired pneumonia develops five episodes of watery diarrhoea in 24 hours and abdominal cramps. She is moved to a side room.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: Confirm the diagnosis: the specific test for the likely organism.
Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in hospital: C. difficile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Send a stool sample for **C. difficile** (GDH and toxin).

elim: AXR looks for toxic megacolon, not the diagnosis.
Blood cultures do not detect C. difficile colitis.
Colonoscopy is unnecessary and risky in colitis.
Calprotectin is for inflammatory bowel disease.

steps.x: **E. Stool C. difficile toxin.** Rule: antibiotic diarrhoea → stool toxin.

practice.e: A stool test for C. difficile toxin confirms the diagnosis. Abdominal X-ray only looks for complications such as toxic megacolon.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man develops a productive cough on day 4 after a hip replacement. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows left lower zone consolidation. Blood and sputum cultures have been sent.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: grade severity, then choose.

clues: Blood and sputum cultures have been sent
steps.x: HAP with normal RR and saturations: non-severe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Non-severe HAP = **co-amoxiclav**.

elim: Piperacillin-tazobactam is for severe HAP.
Amoxicillin alone is the CAP choice.
Clarithromycin alone is CAP or penicillin allergy.
Doxycycline is a CAP alternative.

steps.x: **A. Co-amoxiclav.** Rule: non-severe HAP = co-amoxiclav; severe = pip-taz.

practice.e: Non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia is treated with co-amoxiclav after cultures; piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for severe HAP.

practice.stem: An 81 year old woman on a care of the elderly ward has her first episode of diarrhoea since admission: seven watery stools a day after a course of ceftriaxone. Stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: first or recurrent episode?
First episode of toxin-positive C. difficile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First episode = **oral vancomycin**, plus isolation.

elim: IV metronidazole alone is not first-line.
Fidaxomicin is for recurrence within 12 weeks.
Loperamide risks toxic megacolon.
Oral metronidazole is no longer first-line.

steps.x: **E. Oral vancomycin.** Rule: first C. difficile = oral vancomycin.

practice.e: The first episode of C. difficile infection is treated with oral vancomycin. Fidaxomicin is used for recurrence within 12 weeks.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man with a tunnelled central venous catheter for chemotherapy has had fevers for 3 days despite IV vancomycin. Blood cultures from the line and a peripheral vein both grow Staphylococcus aureus. The exit site is red. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: Next step when antibiotics are failing.

clues: fevers for 3 days despite IV vancomycin
steps.x: Line infection with S. aureus not settling on antibiotics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Source control**: remove the infected line; biofilm protects the bacteria.

elim: There is no chest source.
Oral antibiotics are a step down, not up, in persistent bacteraemia.
Flushing does not clear a biofilm infection.
Cultures grew S. aureus, not fungi.

steps.x: **D. Remove the line.** Rule: device infection not responding = source control.

practice.e: Persistent S. aureus line infection needs the catheter removed, because biofilm protects organisms from antibiotics. Flushing or switching to oral treatment will not clear it.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has a sternal wound infection after cardiac surgery. The wound swab grows Staphylococcus aureus that is resistant to flucloxacillin and all other beta-lactams.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this resistance?
o: Altered penicillin-binding protein encoded by mecA

steps.x: Mechanism of resistance in a named organism.

clues: resistant to flucloxacillin and all other beta-lactams
steps.x: Resistance to all beta-lactams in S. aureus = MRSA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: MRSA: **mecA** encodes **PBP2a**, which beta-lactams cannot bind.

elim: Beta-lactamase is overcome by flucloxacillin, which is beta-lactamase stable.
Efflux pumps are not the cause of methicillin resistance.
Porins are a Gram-negative outer membrane feature.
Ribosomal methylation causes macrolide resistance.

steps.x: **A. mecA / PBP2a.** Rule: MRSA = altered penicillin-binding protein.

practice.e: MRSA carries mecA, encoding PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams. Beta-lactamase alone would not defeat flucloxacillin.
